title: Here we go again – the latest in the Trump tariff saga
gist: With Section 122 balance-of-payments tariffs expiring and the Supreme Court having struck down IEEPA as a taxing authority, the Trump administration pivoted to Section 301 to impose 10–12.5% tariffs on 60 countries over slave-labour import laws, hitting Australia at the top 12.5% rate. The author's structural thesis: US tariffs are permanent because the fiscal position rules out raising other taxes, bond markets are already repricing the deficit, and stablecoin-driven Treasury demand under the GENIUS Act has limits as central bank digital currencies compete.

insights.claim: The Supreme Court ruled that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not give the executive the right to levy taxes, meaning a large share of the "liberation day" tariffs have to be paid back.
insights.speaker: Jenny Gordon
insights.so_what: Refunds are a fiscal cost and a working-capital windfall for importers, but the ruling has redirected rather than ended tariff policy.
insights.locator: even if a large share of the "liberation day" tariffs have to be paid back

insights.claim: As Section 122 temporary tariffs allowed for rebalancing the balance of payments were due to expire, the administration turned to Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act, which permits tariffs on countries assessed as lacking sufficient laws against unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices.
insights.speaker: Jenny Gordon
insights.so_what: The playbook is statute-hopping: each legal defeat prompts a new authority, so tariff exposure should be modelled as persistent regardless of individual court outcomes.
insights.locator: As the Section 122 temporary tariffs allowed for rebalancing

insights.claim: On Thursday the Trump administration announced tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on 60 countries on the basis that they lack adequate laws banning importation of goods made by slave labour, with Australia hit at the higher-end 12.5% rate, up from the current temporary 10%.
insights.speaker: Jenny Gordon
insights.so_what: A concrete 250bp step-up in the Australian tariff rate and a 60-country scope — the specific numbers to feed into exporter margin models.
insights.locator: On Thursday, the Trump administration announced tariffs of 10% to 12.5%

insights.claim: The higher tariffs on Australian exports of steel and aluminium products under the national-security-based Section 232 of the 1962 Trade Expansion Act remain in place alongside the new Section 301 measures, so the burdens stack rather than substitute.
insights.speaker: Jenny Gordon
insights.so_what: Cumulative rather than alternative tariff layers mean effective rates on Australian metals exports are higher than any single announcement implies.
insights.locator: The higher tariffs on Australian exports of steel and aluminium

insights.claim: Australia is not among the 15 countries plus the European Union currently under USTR investigation for unfair manufacturing practices generating a surplus under Section 122, but remains vulnerable to national-security-based investigations.
insights.speaker: Jenny Gordon
insights.so_what: Identifies the residual channel of Australian tariff risk — Section 232 national-security probes, not surplus-based cases.
insights.locator: Australia is not one of the 15 countries

insights.claim: US tariffs are likely here to stay in one form or other because the US political climate makes it very hard for the government to raise taxes, so tariff revenue is too useful to give up.
insights.speaker: Jenny Gordon
insights.so_what: Base case should be structurally higher US tariffs indefinitely, not a reversion trade — reprice supply chains and exporter margins on a permanent basis.
insights.quote: the tariff revenue is just too useful
insights.locator: The US political climate makes it very hard

insights.claim: In the current fiscal environment any source of tax revenue is hard to turn off, especially one that can be politically framed as being paid for by foreigners.
insights.speaker: Jenny Gordon
insights.so_what: The political economy of tariffs is self-reinforcing — the misattribution of incidence is what makes the revenue durable.
insights.quote: In this environment any source of tax revenue is hard to turn off, especially one that can be framed as being paid for by foreigners.
insights.locator: In this environment any source of tax revenue

insights.claim: Congress faces declining options for spending cuts because non-defence discretionary programs are now less than 15% of the US budget, making any revenue source hard to turn down.
insights.speaker: Jenny Gordon
insights.so_what: A hard structural constraint: with discretionary spending under 15% of the budget, tariff revenue has no politically viable substitute.
insights.locator: But for a Congress with declining options for reducing spending

insights.claim: Projections for the US budget deficit are finally scaring bond markets, increasing the cost for the US government of rolling over existing debt on top of financing an ever-growing deficit.
insights.speaker: Jenny Gordon
insights.so_what: Rising rollover costs are the binding constraint driving tariff persistence — watch term-premium and auction dynamics as the transmission channel.
insights.locator: All this comes amid a fiscal reckoning

insights.claim: The GENIUS Act (Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for US Stablecoins Act) has supported and will continue to support growth in the stablecoin market, which creates additional demand for US Treasuries used as stablecoin backing.
insights.speaker: Jenny Gordon
insights.so_what: Stablecoin growth is a real marginal bid for short-dated Treasuries — a structural crypto-to-rates linkage worth sizing.
insights.locator: While the GENIUS Act

insights.claim: There are limits on the rate of stablecoin growth, and central banks in a number of countries are introducing their own digital currencies that will compete with US dollar-denominated stablecoins, capping this avenue for holding down US debt costs.
insights.speaker: Jenny Gordon
insights.so_what: CBDC rollouts are a competitive threat to the stablecoin Treasury bid — a bearish second-order factor for US funding costs and dollar network effects.
insights.locator: Central banks in a number of countries are introducing their own digital currencies

themes.theme: Who actually pays and why tariffs are bad revenue

insights.claim: US consumers and businesses reliant on imported inputs pay the vast share of the tariffs, but these costs are hidden within other sources of rising consumer prices, and politically influential businesses can often negotiate carve-outs.
insights.speaker: Jenny Gordon
insights.so_what: Tariff incidence falls domestically and opaquely — a margin drag on US import-dependent manufacturers, with carve-out access as a differentiator between firms.
insights.quote: it is US consumers and businesses reliant on imported inputs that pay the vast share of the tariffs
insights.locator: While useful to frame tariffs as falling on foreigners

insights.claim: A uniform tariff on all imports can be a sensible revenue tool when other avenues are too hard, but US tariffs are non-uniform with different rates by good and country of origin, forcing businesses to spend more time and effort sourcing least-cost inputs.
insights.speaker: Jenny Gordon
insights.so_what: Rate dispersion, not the level alone, is what destroys value — it creates a permanent sourcing-compliance cost centre for importers.
insights.locator: A uniform tariff on all imports can be a sensible option

insights.claim: Greater uncertainty, rising input costs and rising transaction costs together reduce economic growth, slowing the growth of the US tax base and undermining the fiscal rationale for tariffs.
insights.speaker: Jenny Gordon
insights.so_what: Tariffs are self-defeating fiscally over time — implies eventual pressure toward broader tax reform, though not in the near term.
insights.locator: Greater uncertainty, rising input costs and rising transactions costs

insights.claim: US imports are a fairly small share of the US economy, limiting potential tariff revenue, and higher tariff rates will over time reduce imports and shrink the tax base further.
insights.speaker: Jenny Gordon
insights.so_what: Caps how much fiscal relief tariffs can deliver — deficit projections should not assume tariff revenue scales.
insights.locator: US imports are also a fairly small share of its economy

insights.claim: Rate discretion across goods and countries has given the US bargaining leverage in trade negotiations, meaning the inefficiency of non-uniform tariffs is a deliberate design feature rather than an accident.
insights.speaker: Jenny Gordon
insights.so_what: Because dispersion is intentional leverage, expect continued country-specific carve-outs and deals rather than simplification.
insights.locator: While this discretion has helped the US provide bargaining leverage

insights.claim: There is no gain from retaliation and Australia's best defence is diplomacy and playing by the rules, with policy focus shifting from weathering the US storm to working with others to find calmer waters.
insights.speaker: Jenny Gordon
insights.so_what: Signals no Australian counter-tariff risk — Australian importers and US exporters to Australia face no retaliatory escalation in the base case.
insights.quote: Australia’s policy focus should be less about weathering the US storm, and more on working with others to find calmer waters
insights.locator: With no prospect for a major reversal

insights.claim: Strengthening Australia's 2018 Modern Slavery Act is worth doing on its own merits but is unlikely to see Australia treated any differently by the United States, because the stated tariff rationale is pretextual.
insights.speaker: Jenny Gordon
insights.so_what: Compliance with the stated justification will not buy relief — do not price in tariff removal on the back of legislative fixes.
insights.quote: not because it is likely to see Australia treated any differently by the United States, but because it is the right thing to do
insights.locator: What should Australia do in response

insights.claim: Australia needs to prepare for a world in which US tariffs remain higher and the US continues to use tariffs as an economic weapon to extract concessions from trade partners.
insights.speaker: Jenny Gordon
insights.so_what: Tariff coercion as a standing instrument implies persistent policy risk premium on trade-exposed sectors in US partner economies.
insights.locator: Australia needs to prepare for a world in which US tariffs will remain higher

insights.claim: Most countries have chosen not to respond in kind to the US tariffs, sparing the worst possible outcome of a generalised trade war, and the global economy has been resilient despite being rocked by the US-Israel-Iran war.
insights.speaker: Jenny Gordon
insights.so_what: Non-retaliation is the key reason macro damage has stayed contained — the variable to monitor for regime change to a full trade war.
insights.locator: Most countries have chosen not to respond in kind

insights.claim: Trade and investment can continue driving global growth as long as most countries keep tariffs low and markets open, making cooperation on maintaining the 80-year-old trade and investment rules Australia's core interest.
insights.speaker: Jenny Gordon
insights.so_what: The bull case for global growth is conditional on non-US countries holding the line — watch for defections from open-market policy elsewhere.
insights.locator: Trade and investment can continue to be important drivers
